metaDescription: Six tub transfer benches compared by seat height range, footprint, backrest and weight rating, with the measurements to take before you order for your tub.
introParagraphs: A tub transfer bench solves the single most awkward moment in bathing: lifting a leg over the side of the tub. The bench straddles the tub wall, with two legs outside on the floor and two inside the tub, so you sit down on the outside end and slide across to the inside rather than stepping over. For anyone with limited balance, a stiff hip or a high tub wall, that sideways slide is easier and steadier than a lifted step.

This lineup covers the mainstream designs. The Drive Medical adjusts in half-inch steps and is rated to 350 lb, the Medline lists a 17.6 to 21.9 inch seat height at 400 lb, the HOMLAND uses a thicker-tube A-frame with a 27-inch seat, and the Caring, Dr. Dunley and Medical king round out the 400 lb group. All are tool-free and all have a reversible backrest or a back designed for either side.

We evaluated each from listing specs and buyer feedback, not from hands-on lab work. Before you compare anything, take two measurements: the height of the tub wall from the floor and the width of the tub rim, because a bench that is too wide for the rim or too tall for the wall will not seat correctly on either side.

products.name: Medline Transfer Bench for Bathtubs and Showers, 400 lb
products.description:
The Medline is the most complete everyday bench here. It uses a rust-resistant aluminum frame that weighs 11 lb, adjusts by push button from 17.6 to 21.9 inches and carries a 400 lb rating. A reversible backrest fits on either side of the seat, and a stationary armrest stays on one side for extra support when sitting down or standing up. Wide suction cup feet add security inside the tub and slip-resistant feet hold outside it.

The published dimensions make planning easy: an overall width of 28.7 inches, an overall depth of 18.4 inches and an overall height with the backrest of 32.5 to 36.7 inches. That fairly compact footprint suits a bathroom where floor space beside the tub is limited. The listing puts the seat at 26.5 inches wide, which leaves room for most users.

Assembly needs no tools and the push-button locking legs are easy to set. It sits in the middle of the price range. Compared with the Drive Medical it has a higher rating and an armrest but fewer fine height steps. Choose it as a dependable default for a standard tub. On setup, push each leg button until it clicks, set the height with the user seated and check the feet inside and outside the tub. Wipe the aluminum and seat with a mild cleaner and dry them after each use.
products.bestFor: Standard tubs where a published, compact footprint and an armrest matter.
pros: Reversible backrest with a stationary armrest
cons: Armrest stays on one side only
Height steps are coarser than half-inch designs

products.name: Drive Medical Tub Transfer Bench for Bathtub, Height Adjustable
products.description:
Drive Medical's bench is built around precise height adjustment. Its legs use dual-column extensions that adjust in 0.5-inch steps, which lets you set the seat level with the tub rim more exactly than with coarser push-button designs. The aluminum frame carries a stated 350 lb capacity, with a supportive backrest, drainage openings in the seat and suction cup feet.

Exact height matters on a transfer bench, because a seat that sits even a little below the tub rim creates a bump to slide over, and a seat that is too high makes the user climb. Drainage openings keep water from pooling. The listing says the design suits users who need assistance and promotes stability.

The tradeoff is a lower rating than the 400 lb benches. It sits in the lower-middle of the price range. Compared with the Medline it adds finer height steps but loses 50 lb and the armrest. Choose it when exact seat height is important. Set the legs to the same step on both sides, check the suction cups inside the tub and press the bench with a firm sideways push before use. Dry the drain openings after bathing.
products.bestFor: Tubs where a precise seat height is needed to meet the rim.
cons: 350 lb capacity is the lowest here
Fewer published footprint dimensions in the material we reviewed

products.name: HOMLAND Tub Transfer Bench for Bathtub, 400 lb
products.description:
The HOMLAND uses an A-frame structure with a thicker tube than standard models, which the listing credits for enhanced stability and strength. Seat height adjusts by push button from 17.5 to 22.5 inches, the seat measures 27 by 16.14 inches with drainage holes, and the reversible backrest switches sides for different tubs. The rating is 400 lb and the product is FSA and HSA eligible.

A wide seat and a sturdy frame suit a larger user or anyone who wants a firm feel. The minimum overall width of 32.3 inches and depth of 22.4 inches are larger than the Medline's, so it needs more room beside the tub. The non-slip rubber feet are designed for wet surfaces.

It sits in the middle of the price range. Compared with the Medline it has a wider seat and a stronger frame but a bigger footprint. Choose it when seat size and rigidity matter more than compactness. Because the footprint is larger, test the position before the first shower and make sure it does not block the door or the vanity. Wipe the seat and drain holes, and check the rubber feet for lint and soap film.
products.bestFor: Larger users or anyone who wants a wide seat and a rigid frame.
pros: FSA and HSA eligible per the listing
cons: No armrest mentioned in the material we reviewed

products.name: Caring Transfer Bench, 400 lb
products.description:
The Caring bench pairs a reinforced aluminum frame with an extra-wide ergonomic seat and a supportive backrest, and states a 400 lb capacity. Tool-free adjustable legs let you set the height for your tub, and the bench is reversible for right- or left-side tubs. Rubber-tipped feet create a strong grip on the tub and floor.

The listing is brief on dimensions, so check the product page for seat size and footprint. The extra-wide seat is its main claim, and it suits users who want room to shift while sliding. Tool-free assembly appeals to caregivers.

It sits in the lower-middle of the price range. Compared with the HOMLAND it gives fewer published numbers. Choose it for a simple, wide-seat bench with a standard feature set. Take the time to read the product page for the exact seat size and height range before ordering. Set both sides of the legs level, check the suction feet and wipe the seat after use.
products.bestFor: Users who want an extra-wide seat and a simple tool-free bench.
pros: Reversible for left or right tubs
cons: Few dimensions published in the material we reviewed

products.name: Dr. Dunley Tub Transfer Bench, 400 lb
products.description:
Dr. Dunley emphasizes ease of handling. The listing says the bench supports up to 400 lb, has large suction-cup feet that anchor to the tub or shower surface, assembles by clicking components together without tools and uses a lightweight frame for easier handling by caregivers. The seat is described as generous with a supportive backrest.

A lighter frame is easier to carry, to lift into position and to take out when the bathroom is used by others. The listing gives no height range or dimensions in the material we reviewed, so check the product page before ordering. Large suction feet help the bench stay put once it is placed.

It sits in the lower half of the price range. Compared with the Medline it has fewer published details. Choose it for light weight and quick click-together setup. Because the click-together assembly is quick, take the bench apart for cleaning around the legs now and then. Press the suction cups onto a clean tub floor, and dry the feet after use.
products.bestFor: Caregivers who need a light bench that goes together without tools.
cons: No height or footprint numbers in the material we reviewed

products.name: Medical King Transfer Bench MK7140
products.description:
The Medical King MK7140 is listed as a white plastic bench with adjustable height and a stated 400 lb capacity. The listing describes the experience of sitting on the outside end and sliding over the side of the tub, with a generous seat and backrest for the shower.

The listing is very short, with few specifications, so the product page is where you should look for the seat height range and overall dimensions. A white plastic finish is easy to wipe and does not show the aluminum look of other benches. The lack of detail makes it harder to judge against the Medline or HOMLAND.

It sits in the lower part of the price range. Compared with the others it publishes the least. Choose it only after checking the dimensions against your tub. Check every connection before the first use and confirm the seat height against your tub on the product page. Wipe the plastic dry after use to prevent water from collecting.
products.bestFor: Buyers who prefer a white plastic bench and will verify dimensions first.
cons: Plastic finish and fit are harder to judge from the listing

buyingCriteria.criterion: Measure the tub wall and rim
buyingCriteria.explanation: A transfer bench rests on the tub wall, so its seat height has to clear the rim. Standard tub walls often rise 14 to 20 inches above the floor, so the range matters. The Medline adjusts from 17.6 to 21.9 inches and the HOMLAND from 17.5 to 22.5. Measure the wall height from the floor and the rim width, then choose a seat range that sits level with or slightly above the rim. Take the measurements twice and write them down.

The Drive Medical adjusts in half-inch steps, while the Medline and HOMLAND use push buttons with coarser steps. A seat that is a little low creates a ridge to slide over, and one that is a little high feels like a climb. Finer steps help the final fit, but any bench works if the range covers the rim height. Adjust it with the user seated and test the slide. Try the planned height on a firm chair first, then fine-tune on the tub.

The bench needs floor space beside the tub for its two outside legs. The Medline lists 28.7 by 18.4 inches overall, while the HOMLAND lists a minimum of 32.3 by 22.4. Measure the width of the clear floor beside the tub and the depth to the vanity or wall. A bench that crowds the room is a trip hazard. A tape line on the floor shows how much room the bench will take.

All of these have a reversible backrest, and the Medline adds a stationary armrest that stays on one side. Backrests stabilize the seated user, and armrests give a place to push. Decide which side of the tub the user will enter from, and whether an armrest on that side helps or blocks the slide. Think about transfers with a helper, who may need space on one side.

The legs inside the tub need suction, and the legs outside need slip resistance. The Medline uses wide suction cups inside and slip-resistant feet outside, the Drive Medical suction cup feet, the Caring rubber-tipped suction feet and the Dr. Dunley large suction cups. Suction works best on clean smooth tub floors. Check the feet regularly and wipe soap film away. Replace suction cups when they harden or lose grip.

The Drive Medical states 350 lb and the other five 400 lb. A rating covers the user's weight with the force of sitting and sliding, so leave margin. A thicker-tube frame, like the HOMLAND's A-frame, feels more rigid, and an aluminum frame resists rust. Plastic seats like the Medical King need regular drying. A bench with a cracked seat or a loose leg should be retired right away.

howWeEvaluated.title: Seat height and range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared height ranges from 17.5 to 22.5 inches and the Drive Medical's half-inch steps. Benches that publish a range let you check fit before ordering. A range printed on the listing makes it possible to check fit before ordering.

howWeEvaluated.title: Footprint and published dimensions
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored listings with overall dimensions, such as the Medline's 28.7 by 18.4 inches and the HOMLAND's 32.3 by 22.4. Clear numbers matter because a bench that does not fit is a wasted purchase. A footprint that fits the room is a safety feature, not just a convenience.

howWeEvaluated.title: Support features
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at backrests, armrests and seat width. The Medline's stationary armrest and the HOMLAND and Caring's wide seats were noted. Support features matter most when the user cannot push up easily.

howWeEvaluated.title: Grip and stability
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the feet and frame details: suction and slip-resistant feet, the HOMLAND's thicker-tube A-frame and the Dr. Dunley's large suction cups. Grip details counted for more than appearance.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and ease of setup
howWeEvaluated.description: We recorded the 350 and 400 lb ratings and tool-free assembly across all six. Lightweight frames earned credit for caregivers. Ease of setup was weighed as a caregiver convenience.

faq.q: How does a tub transfer bench work?
faq.a: Two legs stand inside the tub and two stand outside on the floor, with the seat bridging the tub wall. The user sits on the outside end and slides across to the inside, so they never lift a leg over the wall. A caregiver can help with the slide if needed.

faq.q: How do I measure for one?
faq.a: Measure the height of the tub wall from the floor, the width of the rim and the clear floor space beside the tub. Compare to the bench's height range and overall dimensions. The Medline lists 28.7 by 18.4 inches overall, and the HOMLAND 32.3 by 22.4 minimum.

faq.q: What is the difference between a transfer bench and a shower chair?
faq.a: A shower chair sits entirely inside the tub or shower and the user must step in. A transfer bench straddles the wall and lets the user slide in. If lifting a leg over the wall is the problem, choose a bench.

faq.q: Do I need a curtain adjustment?
faq.a: Sometimes. A bench on the tub wall can pinch a shower curtain, and some benches have a cutout to keep curtains inside. A glass door may need to be removed or opened fully. Check your tub setup before ordering.
Yes on all six, so you can set the bench for a left or right entry. The Medline also has a stationary armrest on one side. Decide which side the user enters from first.

faq.q: How do I keep a bench from sliding?
faq.a: Place it on a clean tub surface, press the suction cups down and make sure the outside feet sit flat on a dry floor. Wipe soap film off the feet and the tub. Test the bench with a push before the user sits.

faq.q: Can I use a transfer bench in a walk-in shower?
faq.a: Not as designed. A transfer bench needs a tub wall to straddle. For a walk-in shower, a shower chair or a wall-mounted fold-down seat is the better fit. If you have a tub-shower combination, a bench works well.
